subject: Partial constraints on a multi-normal matrix

messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Partial constraints on a multi-normal matrix
parts:
What’s the best way to set up a 2xN matrix, distributed according to a multi-normal distribution with one column of the matrix constrained to be positive? My thought is a method coded like this, inspired by the example in the missing/partially-known parameters chapter.

parameters{
vector<lower=0>[N] eta_a_raw;
vector[N] eta_b_raw;
}

transformed parameters{
vector[2] eta[N];
for (i in 1:N){
eta[i,1]<-eta_a_raw[i];
eta[i,2]<-eta_b_raw[i];
}
}

model{
for(i in 1:N) eta[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_eta,Sigma_eta);
}

mu_eta is also partially-known, with mu_eta[1] (for the constrained column) estimated from data and mu_eta[2]<-0;, and Sigma_eta estimated from the data in the usual way.

I get a warning during compilation:

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

Warning (non-fatal): sampling statement (~) contains a transformed parameter or local variable.
You must increment lp__ with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
get_base1(eta,i,"eta",1) ~ multi_normal_log(…)

Sometimes this can be ignored, and If I understand correctly, this is one of those cases.

Is this the right way to handle this issue? I’m testing it out and seeing if the results make sense, but I could see ways that this could be conceptually problematic, or at least inefficient. If there’s a better way, I’d love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it’s not the end of the world either, but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.

Thanks all,
Josh

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Partial constraints on a multi-normal matrix
parts:
On Tuesday, May 6, 2014 12:36:29 AM UTC-4, Josh Rosenau wrote:
Is this the right way to handle this issue? I’m testing it out and seeing if the results make sense, but I could see ways that this could be conceptually problematic, or at least inefficient. If there’s a better way, I’d love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it’s not the end of the world either,  but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.

The general rule is that the support of the prior and the parameter (vector) should be the same. So, using a multi_normal distribution when one of the components is strictly positive yields a wrong posterior distribution. It is not so bad if the posterior distribution puts essentially no mass on the negative numbers for that component, but it is hard to know whether that would be the case in advance. In principle, you could get by with a truncated multivariate normal, but Stan doesn't support truncation for multivariate distributions.

I think you have two main options. The first would be to use a multivariate normal distribution for the log of the positive variable and the other variables. You could then antilog as necessary. The other approach would be to use some distribution for positive random variables for the first component and use a conditional multivariate normal for the rest.

Ben

messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Partial constraints on a multi-normal matrix
parts:
Thanks. I recalled that the support of the prior and the parameter ought to be the same, which was part of why I worried this was conceptually problematic. I thought about using the log parameterization, and had been modeling the two variables separately before, but wasn’t sure if I was missing any other ways to make this work. Sounds like there weren’t.

Much appreciated,
Josh

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Partial constraints on a multi-normal matrix
parts:
On May 6, 2014, at 6:36 AM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> What's the best way to set up a 2xN matrix, distributed according to a multi-normal distribution with one column of the matrix constrained to be positive? My thought is a method coded like this, inspired by the example in the missing/partially-known parameters chapter.
>
> parameters{
> vector<lower=0>[N] eta_a_raw;
> vector[N] eta_b_raw;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> vector[2] eta[N];
> for (i in 1:N){
> eta[i,1]<-eta_a_raw[i];
> eta[i,2]<-eta_b_raw[i];
> }
> }
>
> model{
> for(i in 1:N) eta[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_eta,Sigma_eta);
> }

This should work just fine and there's not really an easier
way to do it in Stan. It'd be nice if we coudl vectorize
those assignments, but it wouldn't add any speed --- loops are
already very fast in Stan because they just get compiled to C++.
But right now, we don't yet allow syntax like:

col(eta,1) <- eta_a_raw;

or

eta[,2] <- eta_a_raw;

It's on our to-do list and I hope to get to it this year or
early next year (we're getting pretty backed up in features!).

> mu_eta is also partially-known, with mu_eta[1] (for the constrained column) estimated from data and mu_eta[2]<-0;, and Sigma_eta estimated from the data in the usual way.
>
> I get a warning during compilation:
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
>
> Warning (non-fatal): sampling statement (~) contains a transformed parameter or local variable.
> You must increment lp__ with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
> Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
> get_base1(eta,i,"eta",1) ~ multi_normal_log(...)

>
> Sometimes this can be ignored, and If I understand correctly, this is one of those cases.

I'm not sure what to do about this warning. We may just eliminate
it in the future because it's probably causing more harm than good as is.

The only time you need to adjust for the Jacobian is when there is a non-linear
transform on the left side of a sampling statement. What you have here is
just assignment, but we don't have a good way to track that through
transformed parameters (at least not yet).

>
> Is this the right way to handle this issue? I'm testing it out and seeing if the results make sense, but I could see ways that this could be conceptually problematic, or at least inefficient. If there's a better way, I'd love to know more. If I have to continue treating the two vectors separately, it's not the end of the world either, but the multi_normal approach would capture a meaningful covariance.

Nope --- we don't have a better way of doing this yet. We've been thinking
about adding a constraint syntax that lets each entry of a matrix get its
own lower/upper bounds, but that puts a heavy burden on the data manipulation.

- Bob

Ignore my last comment. In general, always listen to Ben :-)

The way you put together the compound eta is right, but you can't
then sample with variable parameters because it doesn't normalize
the truncation properly.

parts:
We have different expertises. Ben's the expert on multivariate
modeling, linear algebra, and in general on stat modeling issues.
I think he knows more about obscure (some may say "general") distributions
than the rest of us put together. He's the one who came up with the
LKJ distributions for Stan.

I'm the one who built the parser for the language and designed most
of it and most of the code generation (with help, of course --- Marcus
and Daniel have also touched the code, but I think everyone else runs
screaming from the parser).

Marcus wrote the optimizers for point estimates, and also rewrote our
core auto-diff for linear algebra, which gave us a huge speedup.

Daniel's done all the testing and make, as well as writing our error
handling functions and a lot of the code for everything from R-hat
to effective sample sizes. Daniel and I handle the template metaprogramming.

Michael's the geometry expert and expert in HMC (and other sampler
behavior). He's also just insanely good at math. Michael also
wrote the CmdStan command framework (perhaps why it's both
so cool and so non-standard for commands).

Daniel and I are usually the first responders to generic messages
because we're the only two project members being supported to work
on Stan full time and we want to save everyone else's effort for
where it's really needed. Michael's also very active on the list,
and Ben when he's not knee deep in teaching and other projects.

Jiqiang wrote and maintains RStan and Allen wrote and maintains PyStan.

Matt, who's not really active in development any more, but occasionally
joins in on design issues and who we occassionally tap for his deep
algorithm expertise. He wrote NUTS and with me, wrote the very first
prototype for Stan.

Peter Li's our amazing undergrad, who's coming back this summer.
He wrote a ton of code --- almost all of the forward auto-diff and
all of the random-number generators.

- Bob

So, using a multi_normal distribution when one of the components is strictly positive yields a wrong posterior distribution. It is not so bad if the posterior distribution puts essentially no mass on the negative numbers for that component, but it is hard to know whether that would be the case in advance. In principle, you could get by with a truncated multivariate normal, but Stan doesn't support truncation for multivariate distributions.
> > >>
> > >> I think you have two main options. The first would be to use a multivariate normal distribution for the log of the positive variable and the other variables. You could then antilog as necessary. The other approach would be to use some distribution for positive random variables for the first component and use a conditional multivariate normal for the rest.
